say: You give it a sample space and an event. It finds the **probability**: how likely the event is, as a fraction between $0$ and $1$.
The key idea: when every outcome is equally likely, the probability is the number of favourable outcomes over the number of all outcomes.

how.higher: It is a small part or a step inside Paper 2 questions in most years, such as counting pairs or reading a table of outcomes, and the main skill in only 3 parts.
how.ordinary: It is on Paper 2 almost every year, often at the start of Question 1, as 5 or 10 mark parts where you list the outcomes and write favourable over total.

example.question: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores are added. Find the probability that the sum is $9$ or more.

steps.title: Count all outcomes
steps.say: Each die has $6$ faces and any face can go with any face. Multiply to get the total number of outcomes.

steps.title: Count the favourable outcomes
steps.say: List the pairs that give a sum of $9$ or more. Count how many pairs give each sum.

steps.title: Write favourable over total
steps.say: Divide the $\hl{1}{10}$ favourable outcomes by the $\hl{2}{36}$ possible outcomes. Cancel to simplest form.

higher.tip: Count the same way in every part. If you treat pairs as ordered in one part and unordered in the other, you lose marks.

sources.quote: treated as ordered in one part and unordered in the other

higher.tip: Round as the question asks. Wrong or no rounding costs a mark even when the method is right.
A correct answer with no work can still earn full credit, but write the working anyway so a slip does not leave you with nothing.

sources.quote: Accept for full credit correct answers without work

ordinary.tip: A probability is never more than $1$. An answer above $1$ with no work earns zero.
List the outcomes, in a table or a list. Marks are given for the listing, even before you divide.
Pick out the favourable outcomes first. Naming them earns credit even if the rest goes wrong.

say: You give it $n$ different objects to put in a row. It finds the number of **arrangements**: $n!$.
The key idea: the first place has $n$ choices, the next has one fewer, and so on down to $1$. Multiply them.

how.higher: It is a step inside counting questions on Paper 2, such as codes with no repeated digit or arrangements of people, and the main skill in 2 parts.
how.ordinary: It is a 5 to 10 mark part on Paper 2 in 2018 and 2022 to 2025, usually arranging letters, people or routes, sometimes with one item fixed.

example.question: A coach lines up $6$ players for a photograph. In how many different ways can this be done if the captain must stand first?

steps.title: Fix the captain
steps.say: The captain has only one place, so there is $1$ choice for the first spot. That leaves $5$ players for $5$ places.

lines.text: First place: $1$ choice. Remaining places: $5$ players to arrange.

steps.title: Fill the other places
steps.say: The next place has $\hl{1}{5}$ choices, then one fewer each time. Multiply the choices.

steps.title: Write as a factorial
steps.say: A product that counts down to $1$ is a factorial. Work it out.

higher.tip: Each place has one fewer choice, because nothing repeats. Using $9 \times 9 \times 9 \times 9$ for a code with no repeated digits loses a mark.
Listing some correct arrangements earns partial credit. Start listing if you are stuck.
Writing out a factorial in full, such as $(n+3)(n+2)(n+1)\ldots$, earns marks before you simplify.

ordinary.tip: Write the multiplication even if you cannot finish it. Listing the terms without multiplying them still earns marks.

sources.quote: All terms listed but not multiplied

ordinary.tip: Show the multiplication clearly. A correct list with the multiplication indicated earns credit when the answer is not worked out.
Starting to multiply two relevant numbers earns work of merit.

sources.quote: indicates multiplication of two relevant numbers

say: You give it counts for two events in a group. It reads the **Venn diagram** and finds probabilities such as $P(A \cup B)$, $P(A \cap B)$ and $P(A')$.
The key idea: put the overlap in first and subtract it from each circle, so every person is counted once.

how.higher: It appears as a part of Paper 2 probability questions in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2025, often leading to a test for independence, and is the main skill in 3 parts.
how.ordinary: It is on Paper 2 in most years from 2016 to 2024, for 5 or 10 marks, as a Venn diagram, a table or a tree to fill in and then read a probability from.

example.question: In a class of $40$ students, $18$ take drama and $14$ take choir. $6$ students take both. A student is picked at random. Find the probability that the student takes neither drama nor choir.

steps.title: Start with the overlap
steps.say: Write $\hl{1}{6}$ in the part where the circles overlap. Subtract it from each circle to get the parts with one subject only.

steps.title: Add the circles
steps.say: Add the three parts inside the circles. This is everyone who takes at least one subject.

steps.title: Find those outside
steps.say: Everyone not in a circle takes neither. Subtract from the total of $40$.

steps.title: Write the probability
steps.say: Put the $\hl{2}{14}$ students over the $40$ in the class and cancel.

higher.tip: To find $P(A)$, add every number inside circle $A$, including the overlap, and nothing from outside it.

sources.quote: but with no irrelevant numbers added

higher.tip: When checking the addition rule, work out each piece: $P(A \cup C)$, $P(C)$, $P(A \cap C)$. Then substitute. Each correct step earns credit.
Correct table entries earn credit even without working, and each correct value earns marks when the table is incomplete.

sources.quote: Accept correct answers without supporting work

ordinary.tip: A correct filled-in Venn diagram earns full credit without working, and one correct entry already earns marks.

sources.quote: Correctly filled in diagram without work

ordinary.tip: Show the calculation for the overlap, such as adding two circles and subtracting the total. Relevant working earns credit.

sources.quote: Work of merit, for example, some relevant calculation

ordinary.tip: Use your own earlier values. You are marked on consistent work, even when an earlier entry was wrong.

sources.quote: Watch out for consistent work here

ordinary.tip: A probability above $1$ with no work earns zero.

say: You give it $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ for two **independent** events. It finds the probability that both happen: $P(A) \times P(B)$.
The key idea: independent means one event does not change the other, so you can multiply.

how.higher: It is a step inside many Paper 2 probability questions, from 2015 to 2023, as repeated trials, bags of coins or tests for independence, and the main skill in 8 parts.
how.ordinary: It is a 5 to 15 mark part on Paper 2 in most years from 2017 to 2025, usually multiplying probabilities for repeated tries such as three matches or a spinner, and the main skill in 8 parts.

example.question: A fair coin is tossed and a fair six-sided die is rolled. Find the probability of getting a head and a number greater than $4$.

steps.title: Check they are independent
steps.say: The coin does not affect the die. The events are independent, so you can multiply their probabilities.

lines.text: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$ for independent events.

steps.title: Find each probability
steps.say: A head is one of two outcomes. Greater than $4$ means a $5$ or a $6$, two of six outcomes.

higher.tip: Round as asked. Incorrect or no rounding costs a mark on an otherwise correct answer.
Write one correct probability and the multiplication. Even one correct probability earns credit.
The order of the fractions in a product does not matter. Write the full product of correct fractions for high partial credit.

ordinary.tip: Write the layout with full substitution, such as $0.7^3$ or $(0.7)(0.7)(0.7)$. It earns high partial credit.
Multiplying two relevant probabilities earns work of merit, even when you cannot finish.
If you cannot work out the product, write it down. A correct answer indicated but not calculated still earns marks.

sources.quote: Correct answer indicated but not calculated

ordinary.tip: Apply any rounding the question asks for, or you lose a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * for no or incorrect rounding
